title: TruffleHog Secret Detection and Git History Protection
tagline: Deleting a credential from the latest file does not remove it from Git history.
problem: A platform repository needed protection against accidentally committed credentials, including values removed in later commits. Scanner output itself could expose candidate secrets, and running PR-supplied tooling or provider verification would create another trust boundary.
solution: Run a digest-pinned scanner against exact complete Git history or a bounded PR range, using trusted-base tooling and a read-only network-disabled scanner container. Validate completion and coverage, then publish only safe aggregate counts.
outcome: The implementation catches removed history, refuses incomplete coverage and keeps raw candidate fields private. A recorded reconciliation reviewed three detector candidates and confirmed they were public package hashes; it did not create broad secret suppressions.
strengths: Git scanning can find candidate credentials in reachable commits even when the current file has been removed.
Purpose-built detectors identify credential formats. Provider verification is an optional tool capability; this implementation disables it and treats matches as candidates.
Trusted scripts/policy, exact base/head coverage and aggregate-only receipts prevent a candidate change from selecting its own scanner decision or leaking raw output.
limits: A detector match is not proof of a live credential; a public package hash can require independent classification.
A main-history or PR-range scan is not every branch, ref, artifact, image or external mailbox.
Offline means no live validity test
Network none and no-verification reduce exposure, but cannot establish whether a candidate works against a provider.
testcount: 21 passing original contract cases; two optional integration cases are separately recorded
proof: The parser demonstration accepts a fictional candidate and emits only counts. A separate real scanner test uses a disposable repository and an unregistered generated key that is committed and deleted; its exact observed outcome is recorded in Validation. No test key or raw scanner output is published.
